After the brief uproar over Time Warner Cable and Comcast possibly merging, how did DirecTv merging with AT&T slip under the radar?
Time Warner and Comcast are possibly merging? This cannot go well.

They tried, but it didn't go through. Unfortunately...

On May 26, 2015, Charter Communications announced that it would acquire Time Warner Cable for $78.7 billion, along with Bright House Networks in a separate $10.1 billion deal, pending regulatory approval. Charter expects to complete the former transaction by the end of 2015.[8]
because directv isnt another ISP, so them merging with at&t really doesnt change much. so fewer people cared.

AT&T has a knack for staying under the radar. They're one of the worst, if not THE worst cell phone/home ISP out there, but Comcast usually gets more press.

DirecTV is also smaller and offers a specific service AT&T technically doesn't have.

Think of the Comcast and TWC merger as Coke buying Pepsi, or Verizon merging with AT&T. Essentially the top two terrestrial cable/broadband carriers would merge, creating a massive gap between it and all other providers and not just in terms of total subscribers (~33 Million for combined Comcast-TWC vs ~6M for FIOS and U-Verse respectively). There was actually little overlap in the Comcast and TWC service areas, meaning post merger, customers would have the same amount of options as before. The problem however was that Comcast and TWC don't just provide access to content, they create, own, license and negotiate for content as well. Consider everything that would be under the Comcast/TWC umbrella (taken from freepress.net):

  • TimeWarner TV: One television station and the Warner Brothers Television Group; Warner Brothers Television; Warner Horizon Television; CW Network (50 percent stake); TBS; TNT; Cartoon Network; truTV; Turner Classic Movies; Boomerang; CNN; HLN; CNN International; HBO; Cinemax; Space; Infinito; I-Sat; Fashion TV; HTV; Much Music; Pogo; Mondo TV; Tabi; CNN Español

  • Comcast TV : NBCUniversal; twenty-four television stations and the NBC television network; Telemundo; USA Network; SyFy; CNBC; MSNBC; Bravo; Oxygen; Chiller; CNBC World; E!; the Golf Channel; Sleuth; mun2; Universal HD; VERSUS; Style; G4; Comcast SportsNet (Philadelphia), Comcast SportsNet Mid-Atlantic (Baltimore/Washington, D.C.), Cable Sports Southeast, Comcast SportsNet Chicago, MountainWest Sports Network, Comcast SportsNet California (Sacramento), Comcast SportsNet New England (Boston), Comcast SportsNet Northwest (Portland, Ore.), Comcast Sports Southwest (Houston), Comcast SportsNet Bay Area (San Francisco), New England Cable News (Boston), Comcast Network Philadelphia, Comcast Network Mid-Atlantic (Baltimore/Washington, D.C.); the Weather Channel (25 percent stake); A&E (16 percent stake); the History Channel (16 percent stake); the Biography Channel (16 percent stake); Lifetime (16 percent stake); the Crime and Investigation Channel (16 percent stake); Pittsburgh Cable News Channel (30 percent stake); FEARnet (31 percent stake); PBS KIDS Sprout (40 percent stake); TV One (34 percent stake); Houston Regional Sports Network (23 percent stake); SportsNet New York (8 percent stake)

  • TimeWarner Film: Warner Brothers; Warner Brothers Pictures; New Line Cinema; Castle Rock; WB Studio Enterprises, Inc.; Telepictures Productions, Inc.; Warner Brothers Animation, Inc.; Warner Home Video; Warner Premiere; Warner Specialty Films, Inc.; Warner Brothers International Cinemas

  • TimeWarner Other: Warner Brothers Interactive Entertainment; DC Entertainment; DC Comics; Hulu, Fandango

  • Comcast Other: Comcast Interactive Media; Plaxo; Universal Studios Hollywood; Wet 'n Wild theme park; Universal Studios Florida; Universal Islands of Adventure; Philadelphia 76ers; Philadelphia Flyers; Wells Fargo Center; iN DEMAND; Music Choice (12 percent stake); SpectrumCo (64 percent stake)

  • Comcast/TimeWarner Telecom: Clearwire (Combined 14%)

With all of that content under the same umbrella, a combined TWC/TimeWarner would represent a massive shift in power and control over media. Not only would this put them in a superior position to negotiate pricing and contracts with other content providers, but they would be able to demand higher prices for their own content from the remaining competing Broadband/TV providers (U-Verse, Dish, DirecTV, FIOS).

It of course would not stop at content but extend to technology/hardware as well... Comcast, TimeWarner, U-Verse & FIOS all work with companies like Motorola and Cisco for their equipment for example.

When it came to DirecTV & AT&T however, by comparison none of this was an issue.

  • U-verse was a small player in TV, with a small subscriber base (less than 6 million)
  • DirecTV had no broadband offerings of its own.
  • Neither company had any significant ownership or control over content creation.
  • The two companies used completely different technologies

TL;DR, The TWC & Comcast merger represented the merger of two giant, vertically integrated companies, consolidating power that could be used against competing content creators and providers. The AT&T buyout of DirecTV on the other hand represents a horizontal expansion, creating complementary offerings using their respective products.
